reasons: Anchors verified (AVS 18.4 s63, s70; Pindar O. 2.29). akṣita- = ἄφθιτος is exact and *gʷeyh3- underlies jīv-/βίοτος/ζῆν, but formations differ. The relation is not congruent: in Vedic akṣitam is the inexhaustible sustenance one lives on (upa-jīv- 'subsist on', AVS 3.29.8/10, 18.4.63), in Greek ἄφθιτον qualifies life itself (Pindar βίοτον, Eur. Or. 1635 ζῆν). The one noun+epithet match, AVS 7.17.3 jīvātum, is a blessing for the living, not an afterlife text. The afterlife setting is a real but loose parallel, and 'imperishable life' for the immortalised is an obvious coinage.

All 8 anchors verified. εὐρύς = urú- is exact; πόντος ~ pánthā- (*pónteh1-/pn̥th1-) is the standard equation and the drift 'path' > 'sea' is defensible. But 'wide' is a generic sea epithet in Greek: in Homer εὐρύς goes with θάλασσα (12 lines, 0.7 expected) at least as much as with πόντος (9, 0.8 expected), and πόντος has stronger fixed epithets (οἶνοψ 15, ἀτρύγετος 8). In the RV urú- + pánthā- is 4 genuine pādas (5.1.11c is not attributive). So each side is an ordinary noun-epithet pairing. The argument that a Greek poet would not need the old path word fails, because πόντος is simply one of Greek's main sea words. Possible, not demonstrated.

Anchors verified. In Ion the words are in line 41, not the anchor line 42. Both pairs are cognate (sū́ra-/sū́rya- ~ ἥλιος; cakrá- = κύκλος) and the RV mythologem is formulaic (7 pādas: Indra tearing off the sun's wheel). But Greek ἡλίου + κύκλος is absent from Homer. It appears in tragedy and Herodotus and then in astronomical prose (Autolycus, Aristotle), where κύκλος means 'disc, orbit'. Calling the sun a circle with the language's ordinary 'circle' word is generic. Only the Ion 'riding' passage hints at a vehicle-wheel image. The Vedic wheel (of the sun's chariot) and the Greek disc are not clearly the same image.

Anchors verified (Il. 9.261; Laurentian Chronicle 61.22). δῶρον ~ darъ and δίδωμι ~ dati are cognate, but 'give gifts' with the -ro- derivative of the same root is a figura that any language with such a noun forms on its own. The Old Russian chronicle is also open to Byzantine Greek influence. The contexts (gifts offered to Achilles, gifts to Olga) share nothing beyond the act of giving.

Anchors verified. The two Aristotle loci are quotations of Il. 18.109, not a separate Greek witness (Plato Philebus quotes it too). μέλι = mel is exact. de Vaan doubts γλυκύς ~ dulcis as PIE (an ad hoc assimilation, perhaps a common loan), so etymology_ok is false for the 'sweet' slot. The comparative 'sweeter than honey' is near-universal, so the ordinary words for 'sweet' and 'honey' are bound to co-occur. Plautus adapts Greek comedy and Lucretius' honeyed cup is a Greek topos, so the Latin is not clearly independent. The Vedic match renews both lexemes and is thematic only. The speech/endearment application is the one point of interest.

reasons: Anchors verified (Solon in Ath. Pol. 12.4; Plaut. Cas. 971; Catull. 108.6). κύων ~ canis is cognate (vocalism irregular). lupus ~ λύκος is not a straightforward cognate pair: de Vaan needs metathesis plus a Sabellic loan, or derives it from another root. The figures differ: Solon is a wolf turning at bay among dogs; Plautus means 'wolves here, dogs there', trapped between two dangers; Catullus is carrion-eaters. Wolf and dog are a natural pair for any herding culture, so this is generic.

reasons: Anchors verified. dhr̥ṣ- = θαρσ- and mánas- = μένος are sound. Vedic dhr̥ṣát + mánas is formulaic (RV 1.54.3b, 5.35.4c, 8.62.5a; dhr̥ṣánmanas-), and Homer has μένος + πολυθαρσές 3x (Il. 17.156, 19.37, Od. 13.387). But the Greek anchor Il. 16.242 has ἦτορ, not μένος. The Greek adjective is a πολυ- compound. The semantics diverge: an Indra-type 'bold mind' versus fighting-force that a god puts into a hero. 'Bold spirit' from the ordinary words for boldness and spirit is close to generic, so this is suggestive only.

Anchors verified (Il. 4.27; RV 10.106.10c; the two Hippocratic sentences). ἱδρώς/ἱδρόω ~ svéda-/svid- is correct. The cognate-accusative 'sweat a sweat' is unique on each side (Homer 1 line, RV 1 pāda), and both poetic loci are about toil. But the cognate accusative is productive in both languages, Greek ἱδρόω is a denominative of the noun (an independent formation), and the Hippocratic dative of manner is clinical prose. Shared figure, plausibly independent.

reasons: Anchors verified. AVP 19.16 s21 does not contain dīrgham/āyus; they are in s22. The Lucretius lines are irrelevant (aevum 'age' with durare). Only one element is cognate (αἰών ~ ā́yus ~ aevum, by root with different stems). 'Long' is renewed (δηρός vs dīrghá-), and dūrāre with *dweh2- is doubtful. 'Long life' is as generic as a phrase can be.

Anchors verified (Plato Theaet. 158c = GLAUx s433; Lysis 204d = s32; RV 10.164.3b; AVS 6.96.3). The *h1ger- reduplicated stem (ἐγρήγορα ~ jāgāra) and *swep- (ὕπνος ~ svap-) are cognate. But in Theaetetus the sleep member is renewed by καθεύδω, so the merism is not lexically shared. The narrower sub-formula 'wake from sleep' (sleep noun in the ablative + *h1ger- verb: Hom. Il. 2.41, Lysis, Av. HN 1.13) is real, but Avestan varies the verb in the same frame (HN 1.11 and VS 18.49 with other verbs). Waking/sleeping and 'wake from sleep' are universal pairings of the ordinary words.

Anchors verified (AVS 2.28.7, AVP 1.12.5, AVS 3.23.14, 12.1.26; Lucr. 2.610). Lucr. 2.610 concerns the Phrygian Magna Mater and has no Father member. In Latin only the kinship terms are cognate (Pater + aether, Matris + terrai Lucr. 1.250, 2.992). Lucretius here follows Greek philosophical models (Euripides), so the Latin is derivative. The real inherited item *dyeus ph2ter (dyauṣ + pitā = Iuppiter = Ζεῦ + πάτερ) is not in the anchors, and Earth's name is renewed everywhere. Sky-father + earth-mother as parents is also typologically widespread. The Vedic side is strongly formulaic, but the cross-branch phrase is not shown here.

Anchors verified. RV 10.123.3d has the noun only, no 'sweet'. μέθυ = mádhu- and ἡδύς = svādú- are exact. Homeric μέθυ + ἡδύ is formulaic (9 lines, 0.03 expected). But the Vedic side barely has the attributive pair: RV 1.187.2a has vocatives of pitu- ('food'), with mádhu- used adjectivally; 3.31.11d and 10.29.6d use the noun svā́dman; 8.49.4b is a partitive superlative. 'Sweet' with honey or a sweet drink is the most natural collocation, and Greek also says ἡδύς of οἶνος, so the Greek pair need not be inherited.

Anchors verified (Arist. De color. = GLAUx s195 and EN 1099b = s254; AVS 8.2.55; Cato 138.1). βοῦς/gó-/bōs and ἵππος/áśva-/equus are exact cognates. But listing the main domestic animals, in prose taxonomy (Aristotle), a farm regulation (Cato) and a blessing (AVS), is what any herding society's language does with its ordinary words. The structures and functions are not congruent. The Vedic gó- + áśva- pair is formulaic only on its own side.

reasons: Anchors verified. amṛ́ta- = ἄμβροτος and vas- = ἕννυμι (*wes-) are exact. But the relation differs: Greek ἄμβροτος is an adjective on the garment noun, 'divine clothes' (6 Homeric lines, also of living gods: Od. 7.265, Il. 14.178), while Vedic amṛ́ta- is the substance one is clothed with. On the Vedic side this occurs only in RV 6.75.18 (= AVS 7.118.1) and AVS 9.1.2: in RV 2.10.1 amŕ̥ta- is the subject Agni, and in 9.94.4 amr̥tatvám is the goal of a motion verb, not worn. The warrior-protection parallel (armour charm vs Sarpedon's corpse) is suggestive, but both *n̥mr̥tó- reflexes attach to many divine things, and Vedic vas- 'wear' takes many abstract objects.

Anchors verified. The underlying formula is real: agent noun *deh3-tor- + gen. pl. of *h1wesu- (Od. 8.325 and 8.335, Hes.; RV 8.51.5a; Av. Y16.1b, Y65.12b; Av. dātar- is ambiguous between 'giver' and 'creator'). But this claim's anchors do not carry it. In Il. 24.528 ἑάων depends on δώρων ('gifts of goods') with the finite verb, not the agent noun. YtFra8.2e has only an adjective vaŋᵛhīš with no giver at all. Accepted as phraseology elsewhere (see B053); weak as anchored here.

Anchors verified. Od. 8.335 has the exact agent noun + gen. pl. of *h1wesu- (also Od. 8.325, of the gods). RV 8.51.5a dātā́ + vásūnām and Av. Y16.1b, Y65.12b and Y65.13b dātar- + vohunąm match it exactly (both members cognate, same syntax, divine epithet in hymnic address). Greek ἐΰς is a living adjective in Homer, but its substantive 'goods' sense is confined to this genitive plural, a fossil that argues against independent creation. Caveats: the Vedic anchors RV 7.6.7a (ā́-dā- 'take') and AVP 19.1.5 (vasupati-) are only loosely related, and Av. dātar- could be 'creator' (*dʰeh1-).

Anchors verified (Arist. Protrepticus = GLAUx s269; RV 10.164.3b; AVS 6.45.3, 6.96.3, 6.115.3, 7.108.3, 8.6.15). The Vedic merism is a fixed expiation/protection formula. The Greek anchor is a philosophical contrast (dream images false, waking true) in which the sleep verb is καθεύδω and *swep- appears only as the noun. A waking/sleeping opposition built from the ordinary verbs is universal. Function and wording are not congruent.

reasons: Anchors verified (h.Ven. 282; AVP 5.5.4; RV 10.184.1d). Only the verb *dʰeh1- is shared, and it is the default 'put' verb in both. The object differs (Vedic gárbha- 'embryo' vs Greek υἱός/παῖς 'under the girdle'). Vedic gárbhaṃ + dhā- 'conceive' is formulaic, but Greek attests the construction only in this hymn. The middle with a mother as subject is a modest point of congruence.

Anchors verified. Od. 11.330 does not have the claimed pair: ἄμβροτος qualifies νύξ and φθῖτο is a positive finite verb ('the night would waste away'), a different idea. The coordinations cited (Eur. Andr., h.Merc.) use non-cognate ἀθάνατος. RV 9.113.7d amṛ́ta- + ákṣita- + loká- has no Greek counterpart with both cognates, and coordinated privatives are a common figure anyway.

Anchors verified (Catull. 61.76; Od. 21.50). pando ~ πετάννυμι and claustrum (claudo) ~ κληΐς are cognate (de Vaan: *pt-n-h2-, *kleh2u-d-). But the words do not stand in the same relation: Latin has an imperative with the bolts as object; in Greek the doors are the passive subject and the key is an instrument. The contexts differ (a wedding call vs Penelope unlocking a storeroom). Doors, bolts and opening are everyday co-occurrences. Catullus 61 also works with Greek epithalamium models.

Anchors verified (RV 1.103.4d; Simonides Ep. 7.514.4, with κλεεννόν in line 3). The core *h1nómn̥ + dʰeh1- (nā́ma + dhā- ~ ὄνομα + θέσθαι, Od. 18.5) is a genuine inherited idiom, but the relations differ. Vedic is the middle 'took on a name for fame' (purpose dative of śrávas-). Greek is the factitive 'made (his father's) name famous', τίθημι with a predicate adjective. sūnú- and υἱός share the root but not the suffix (*suHnu- vs *suHyu-). The extra 'son' and 'fame' elements are natural companions of 'name', so beyond the known naming idiom the match is not compelling.

All 5 anchors verified. θύρα = foris, and the Greek and Latin bolt-verbs both go back to *kleh2w- (Greek κληΐω is a denominative of κληΐς; Latin claudo, per de Vaan *kleh2u-d-, is formed separately). The phrase is 'shut the doors' / 'open the doors' with each language's ordinary words. The claim itself says the bolt-verbs may be independent, and Catullus has ianua, not fores. Co-occurrence of the ordinary 'close' and 'door' words is expected, so the higher-than-chance counts do not show inheritance.

Anchors verified (Cato 141.3; AVS 1.31.7; AVP 1.22.7). The anchors are renewed (Latin pastores for *wiHro-; the AV verse has go- and puruṣa-), but the formula is solidly attested in the support, which I checked. Umbrian Iguvine Tables VIa 30-32 (Buck lines 14789-14820) have ueiro + pequo as beneficiaries with saluo + seritu, the same cognate verb and adjective as Cato's salua + seruassis. Av. YtFra2.10e and VrS18.3c have pasu- + vīra- for protection and peace. AVP 19.56 s26, s30 and s32 have paśu- + vīra- in a well-being prayer. Both members are cognate in coordination, in prayers for protection of a community, across Italic and Indo-Iranian. The Cato anchor keeps *peḱu and the protection frame. The merism is plausible among herders, but the agreement extends to the verb and adjective of keeping safe (in Italic).

Anchors verified (AVS 7.62.2; Eur. Ion 5). nā́bhi- ~ ὀμφαλός share the root *h3nobʰ- with different suffixes. 'Earth' is renewed (pṛthivī́- vs γῆ). Both sides are formulaic: RV nā́bhi- + pṛthivī́- in 9 units (0.44 expected); Greek γῆς + ὀμφαλός of Delphi. Both use it of a cult centre, which is a real point. But navel-of-the-world imagery is cross-culturally common, and only one element is cognate.

Anchors verified (Eur. Ion 410, IA 1487; AVS 7.6.3). πότνια = pátnī- and μήτηρ = mātár- are cognate, but there is no congruent collocation. In AVS 7.6.3 mātár- and pátnī- are separate appositions, each with its own genitive (mother of the Ādityas, mistress of ṛta). The pair never occurs in the RV, and Greek πότνια is an honorific epithet of μήτηρ. IA 1487 addresses a human mother. One isolated Vedic co-occurrence is chance.

Anchors verified (Il. 22.66, with ὠμησταί in line 67; AVS 8.6.48; RV 1.162.10b; AVS 8.4.4). ὠμός = āmá- and the root *h1ed- are exact. The decisive match is the compound 'raw-eater' (Gk ὠμηστής, Ved. āmā́d-) with the same use: in RV 10.87.7d the raw-eating birds are to devour the sorcerer; in Il. 11.454 and 22.67 the raw-eating birds and dogs tear the enemy's corpse. Same scene and curse register, and both members cognate in the same order. Vedic kravyā́d- (flesh-eater; RV 7.104.2, 10.87.2/19) is the parallel compound on the cognate of κρέας. Caveat: the Greek agent formation in -ηστής differs from the Vedic root noun, and 'raw-eater' compounds are easy to coin, so the risk is medium.

Anchors verified (RV 9.61.10c; Pindar I. 7.29). Neuter máhi = μέγα and śrávas- = κλέος are exact in form, and the attributive neuter noun phrase is formulaic on both sides: máh- + śrávas- in 16 RV pādas (1.8 expected; 11 with exactly the two words), μέγας + κλέος in 13 Homeric lines (1.7 expected; Il. 6.446, Od. 1.240). In both, fame is a prize won or increased. 'Great fame' is semantically natural, but the agreement in both the form and the noun phrase, with fame as a poetic value, makes this the clearest match in the batch.

Anchors verified. AVS 10.6.35 lacks akṣita (it is in s34), and AVS 7.17.3 has akṣita with 'life', not water. ákṣita- = ἄφθιτος is exact, but the water nouns are renewed or are different derivatives (ὕδωρ vs útsa- from *wed-; ā́p- non-cognate). Greek has ἄφθιτον + ὕδωρ once (Styx). 'Unfailing spring/water' is a natural phrase. The Vedic útsa- + ákṣita- is formulaic, but the Greek match is a single and differently motivated instance.

Anchors verified (Il. 1.441; RV 1.38.1b; AVS 7.9.7; Dem. The prose anchors are everyday legal narrative. Generic.

Anchors verified (Arist. De div. 1 s22; AVS 6.115.3, 6.45.3). Same as B054: the Aristotle passage contrasts perception in sleep and waking (ὕπνοις vs ἐγρηγορέναι) in technical prose.
